title: Strawbridge v. Curtiss (1806)
summary: The Court construed the diversity statute to require the complete diversity described in the casebook’s jurisdictional framework.
notes: Do not use this short note to invent the underlying transaction or a modern exception. Compare statutory interpleader and the Class Action Fairness Act for separately authorized jurisdictional arrangements.

sections.Parties: The assigned note addresses parties seeking federal jurisdiction on the basis of diverse state citizenship.
sections.Material Facts: The jurisdictional arrangement involved parties on opposing sides whose citizenship did not satisfy the complete-diversity construction. The casebook uses the decision primarily to explain the statutory rule; it does not reproduce a detailed factual account of the underlying substantive controversy.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court rejected the asserted statutory jurisdiction. The assigned treatment is a short historical note.
sections.Issue: How broadly did the statutory grant permit federal jurisdiction when multiple parties appeared on each side?
sections.Holding: The grant required the form of complete diversity that became the conventional rule for ordinary diversity actions.
sections.Reasoning: The case is about construction of the statutory grant, not the maximum power Article III allows Congress to confer. That distinction explains why later statutes may authorize minimal diversity in particular settings. It also explains why the citizenship of every relevant party ordinarily must be considered before invoking ordinary diversity jurisdiction.

learning.why: The Court construed the diversity statute to require the complete diversity described in the casebook’s jurisdictional framework.

topics.cp-diversity: The decision is the source of the complete-diversity construction discussed in the course.
topics.cp-statutory-constitutional: The statutory requirement is narrower than the constitutional permission for minimal diversity.
